h1: Negotiating a distributor agreement for craft beer in India
title: Craft Beer Distributor Agreements | Craft Beer School
desc: The terms that matter in a craft beer distributor deal in India: territory, credit, cold storage, rotation, targets and exit, plus how state routes differ.
teaser: The distributor wants exclusivity and ninety days' credit. You want your beer cold and your money back. Both can be negotiated.
standfirst: A distributor can make a small brewery or quietly bankrupt it. The difference is usually in the terms nobody read closely. Here is what to negotiate and why.
sections: Know which route your state uses

In India the route to market for beer depends on the state. In some states a government corporation buys beer from breweries and supplies retailers, so the brewery's commercial relationship is largely with that corporation. In others, licensed private distributors or wholesalers sit between brewery and outlet. A few states mix both. Our guide to beer distribution in India explains the main models.

Negotiation only exists where you have a choice. Where the state corporation sets the terms, your work is on pricing approval, registration and supply reliability. Where private distributors operate, the agreement below matters a great deal.

Distributors often ask for exclusive rights across a city or state. Exclusivity can make sense if they commit to real effort in return. Tie it to performance: minimum volumes, number of active outlets plus the right for you to end exclusivity if targets are missed for a set period. Define the territory precisely. Specify which channels they cover, for example bars and restaurants, retail shops or both. Our guide to on-trade versus off-trade explains why the two behave differently.

Credit terms decide your cash flow. Long credit periods are common in Indian liquor trade and a small brewery can end up financing its distributor. Negotiate the credit period, what happens when payments are late, whether interest applies and your right to stop supply. Agree how payments are reconciled and how often. Ask for security deposits or advance payment for new partners.

Then model the worst case. If the distributor pays at the very end of the credit period, how much cash does your brewery need to keep brewing? If that number frightens you, the terms are wrong.

Craft beer is far more sensitive to heat and age than most of what a typical liquor distributor handles. Write the handling into the agreement:

  • Storage temperature in the warehouse and in transit.
  • First in, first out rotation by packaging date.
  • Maximum age of stock delivered to outlets.
  • Who pays for stock that goes out of date or is damaged by heat.
  • Your right to inspect the warehouse.

Breakage, returns and expired stock are where disputes start. Settle them on paper before the first truck leaves.

Agree the distributor's margin clearly, how price changes are handled when excise or costs move and who funds promotions, samples and point-of-sale material. Price must stay within the approved MRP and your state's rules on schemes and discounts. Our beer pricing strategy guide shows how to build the price waterfall from brewery gate to shelf.

Ask what the distributor will actually do: how many sales staff, which outlets they visit, how often they will report sales by outlet. A distributor who carries two hundred brands may not sell yours without help.

Insist on regular sales reporting by outlet, not just a monthly total. You want to know which bars and shops reorder, which ones stopped and how long stock sits in the warehouse. Agree the format and frequency in the contract, ideally weekly or fortnightly. Ask for stock-on-hand reports by packaging date so you can see ageing stock before it becomes a write-off.

Without this data you cannot judge the distributor's performance or plan production. With it you can spot a problem outlet early, send your own team to help and give the distributor targets that mean something. A distributor who refuses to share outlet data is telling you something about how the relationship will run.

Start with a short initial term and a clear renewal process. Define how either side can end the agreement, the notice period and what happens to stock, kegs and unpaid invoices at the end. Make sure kegs and branded equipment remain yours and come back.

Have a lawyer review the final draft. A distribution agreement is a legal contract with long consequences. This guide is not legal advice. What you bring to the table, though, is commercial clarity: your volumes, your margins and the cash you can afford to tie up.
faqs: Do all Indian states allow private beer distributors?
No. Some states route beer through a government corporation, others use licensed private distributors and some mix both. Check how your state works.
Should I give a distributor exclusivity?
Only if they commit to targets in return, with your right to end exclusivity if they miss them for a set period.
It depends on your cash position and the market norm. Model the worst case where they pay at the end of the period and make sure your brewery can survive it.
